newsitem.title: UK: UK's Oftel, BT to step up school deal talks.
newsitem.headline: UK's Oftel, BT to step up school deal talks.

text.p: UK telecoms watchdog Oftel and British Telecommunications Plc will meet on Friday for further talks about BT's proposals to offer competitive Internet computer access to schools, BT said.
Acceptance of the proposals could help BT win an early release from a current ban on it using its extensive network for potentially lucrative entertainment services, analysts say.

The new Labour government -- which wants telecoms companies to rapidly roll out the sophisticated networks needed for high-speed communications across the country -- has said the timing of lifting the ban depends on how BT will improve access to the information superhighway.
But Oftel insists that there is no link between BT offering cheap computer deals to schools and a change to broadcast policy.
"In Oftel's eyes, this is completely separate," an Oftel spokeswoman said.

Oftel wants schools to have access to high speed networks that can support 10-20 computers hooked up to the Internet computer network at any one time, as well affordable prices and a choice of service provider.
Cruickshank is publishing a consultative document in July on BT's proposals and possible alternatives, to ensure that better services for schools are not delayed.

BT, which has been upgrading its network, said it had developed packages of particular interest to primary and some secondary schools which it wanted to offer across the country in time for the start of the autumn term.
The company welcomed news that Cruickshank was ready to push forward its proposals, saying it wanted to start offering new services as early as possible.
"We are pleased they (Oftel) are taking things forward," a company spokeswoman said.
Although BT declines to detail the price of packages it is offering, Oftel said in a statement that they were similar to those of its rivals -- the cable companies.
Cable groups have introduced special school packages which broadly give schools unlimited access to the Internet for one pound per pupil per year. -- Kirstin Ridley, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7987
